newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries higher at midday on weak sales data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries higher at midday on weak sales data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices were higher at midday on Thursday after government data on spring U.S. retail sales seemed all but to eliminate the chance of another Federal Reserve interest rate hike in July.

The Commerce Department said retail sales slipped 0.1 percent in May, contrary to forecasts for a 0.4 percent gain. An even sharper 0.9 percent drop in April retail sales, revised from the 0.3 percent decline first reported, bolstered the view that consumers spent the last three months recovering from a brisk shopping spree early in the year, analysts said.
Weekly data on new jobless claims released by the Labor Department at the same time as the retail sales data did not spoil the picture of a weaker economy.

New jobless claims, which surged higher in the week containing the Memorial Day holiday, were expected to reverse at least some of that increase this week. Instead, fresh claims for state unemployment insurance rose to 339,000 in the week ended June 7, up from 338,000 new claims a week earlier.
At midday, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 26/32 to 98-2/32, yielding 6.78 percent. The bond was up 6/32 before the data came out, helped by a stronger dollar.

Minutes after the retail sales data were released, the 30-year benchmark Treasury bond climbed to a full point gain before trimming about a quarter of its advance and trading steadily at that level through midday.

Joshua Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust, said the retail sales data "almost assuredly" clinched the outcome of the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) policy meeting in July as one from which no interest rate hike would emerge.
"The markets and the Fed are all taking comfort in the fact that the economy slowed in the second quarter," he said.
The receding likelihood of a Fed rate hike gave a good boost to the short end of the maturity curve.

At noon EDT/1600 GMT, three-month bill rates were down one basis point to 4.83 percent but six-month rates were down six basis points to 5.14 percent and year bill rates were off nine basis points to 5.36 percent.
The spread between the Federal funds rate of 5-1/2 percent and the two-year note yield had narrowed to 58 basis points by noon EDT, from 68 basis points at the close on Thursday.
Traders said a hedge fund unwound a curve-flattening trade, buying shorter maturities and selling at the long end.
But analysts said the possibility that economic activity would pick up again in June and in the third quarter was keeping the market's advance from becoming a runaway rally.

"Certainly these numbers today were weaker than some people expected," said David Sloan, senior economist at I.D.E.A. "They do signfiicantly reduce the chance of a Fed tightening in July, although I don't think they removed the risk of a Fed tightening in August."
Sloan said I.D.E.A. believes that a strong economic trend would reemerge in the second half of the year.

"Weakness in the second quarter (when the weather was unseasonably cool) was a partial reversal of a strong first quarter when the weather was supportive for the consumer," said Sloan. "(We have) to see how things work out in June."
"The real question is what the trend will be in the second half of the year," said Feinman. "Our view is that the economy still has a lot of underlying momentum."
Five-year notes were priced at 100-19/32, up 14/32, at midday to yield 6.36 percent. Ten-year notes were trading at 100-31/32, up 19/32, to yield 6.49 percent.
